prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level
for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: I move from a single-candidate view to a two-part prize that pairs the two cases where a discovery or invention is unambiguous and where the credited names are cleanest. Optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) are a concrete invention that is reproduced at many national metrology institutes and has taken fractional uncertainty to the 10^-18 level, with consequences for the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. The three colleagues who ranked it in their top three (Kroll, Lindroth, and I) were each looking at the same properties: a simple, original idea, a two-name credit set that maps exactly onto proposal and realisation, and independent confirmation. IceCube's detection of a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos, and the later evidence for TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane, opened a new observational window on the universe. It required a new detector concept built in Antarctic ice over decades, and the result is a discovery about nature, not a refinement. Together the two parts span precision measurement and observational astroparticle physics, contain three people in total, and avoid choosing between the many contested credit splits that dominate the other strong candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that Halzen alone is the only credited name for IceCube, a collaboration of hundreds, and a sole credit for a collaborative instrument is hard to defend without recognising the other builders and leaders of AMANDA and IceCube; that weakens this part and is the main reason I put B044 as an alternative. Source-level associations are still at roughly 4 to 5 sigma for a handful of objects and independent confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD is still developing, so one could argue the diffuse-flux discovery is mature but the astronomy is not. For the clock part, the 2005 and 2012 prizes already covered frequency combs and ion control, so the committee may see lattice clocks as a refinement of recognised metrology. Finally, B044 has by far the broadest opening support (four top-three placements), and a configuration that leaves it out has to justify why.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B044) first, calling it a clean prediction followed by a decisive experiment, and judged the recognition overdue, while also flagging the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit and the 2016 overlap as a real allocation question.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously and it is why I list B044 as my first alternative. But your own uncertainty is the heart of my hesitation: the HgTe/CdTe experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which is outside the credited set, and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Roy overlaps with it. Eriksson, Johansson and Kroll each raise the same missing names. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be defensible only if the committee is prepared to defend leaving BHZ out, and I would want that settled before putting it at the centre. Opening support is not scientific merit, and four top-three placements do not resolve the attribution problem.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics, with Katori and Ye as the only names needed and many independent labs confirming performance.
responses.response: I agree with the credit and the maturity argument, and the two-name set is the cleanest among all shortlisted candidates. I would qualify your framing slightly: your own note that the prize may look like an engineering refinement of the Hall and Wineland recognitions is a fair worry, and I do not think it is answered by listing the redefinition of the second, which has not yet happened. I would like the citation to emphasise the invention of the magic-wavelength lattice itself, not simply a record accuracy figure. Given that, I think it is strong enough to carry half a prize, which is why I propose pairing it rather than treating it as a stand-alone.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked lattice clocks first and optical-lattice quantum simulation (B004) second, but flagged that choosing three from five credited names leaves out well-deserving contributors, and that the scientific payoff of quantum simulation is about methods more than a single new phenomenon.
responses.response: I agree with your reservation about B004 and it is why I keep it at the bottom of my own list. Choosing among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Dalibard is arbitrary to some degree, and the overlap with the 2001 and 1997 prizes plus the Cirac and Zoller appearances in the trapped-ion candidate make any three-name subset fragile. I part company with you on the moire candidate B020, which you ranked fourth: you note the superconductivity mechanism is disputed, which for me means the interpretation is not yet stable enough, so I rank it below the clocks even though replication is excellent.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B042) first as the architecture behind essentially all superconducting processors, noting that Blais is the main casualty of a three-person limit and that overlap with last year's prize may be seen as too close.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is a very mature and influential line, but it is the kind of case where the instrument is the achievement, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject. Your own flagged uncertainty about Blais versus Girvin on the theory side and your declared professional proximity to this community both argue for caution before making it central. I also note that only you ranked it, so I would want a stronger case from the other members before it displaces a candidate with broader support.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked dynamical mean-field theory (B037) first on originality and decades of impact, and acknowledged that Metzner and Muller-Hartmann are missing from the credited set and that DMFT is a method rather than a single discovery.
responses.response: The impact is real, but I would give weight to the second half of your own caveat. A framework or method whose early history involves two uncredited names and whose three-person set leaves out Metzner is a harder prize to frame as a discovery or invention. I would not rule it out, but it sits behind candidates with a clean observable result.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend a sole credit for Halzen on IceCube, or whether an IceCube configuration is only viable if additional names beyond the supplied credit can be introduced, which the protocol does not allow here.
Whether B044 should be preferred over my configuration given its much broader opening support, which depends on how the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission is weighed.
Whether lattice clocks are judged distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
I rely on my own recollection of IceCube source significances and of the timeline for redefining the second, and have not independently verified either.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for either part. My documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) are not IceCube or optical-clock projects, but as an astroparticle experimentalist I work in a neighbouring community to IceCube and I flag that field proximity for the committee to judge; as Chair I will not let it affect procedure.
